newsitem.title: ITALY: FAO says Third World needs major food help.
newsitem.headline: FAO says Third World needs major food help.

text.p: The global food situation has improved but war and famine have hit some of the world's poorest nations who need large-scale assistance, the U.N. Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO) said on Monday.

Hunger also continued to hit the youngest hard, with one in three children under the age of five in the developing world being classed as underweight. However, fewer people were facing shortages than 20 years ago.

"Fifty-six percent of all deaths of children under five -- 18,000 a day -- are directly or indirectly caused by malnutrition," Hartwig de Haen, FAO's assistant director general for economic and social affairs, told a news conference.
His comments followed release of two new FAO reports drawn up before the crisis in eastern Zaire, which has left more than a million starving refugees with no access to food or water.
The reports were published to coincide with a World Food Summit in Rome this week, which will set reliable food supplies for all as the international community's goal.
Its declaration will commit leaders to reducing the number of undernourished people in the world to half its present level of around 840 million by no later than 2015.
That figure in itself marked an improvement from the 918 million people who were undernourished in 1969-71 when there were 1.5 billion fewer people in the developing countries.
FAO hailed a general improvement in food supplies in 1996 but said there was no reason for real optimism.
"Even in a year of very good crops, record crops, we're still worried," James Greenfield, director of FAO's commodities and trade division, told a news conference.
"If we have a poor crop next year we will be back to exactly the same situation as in 1995/96," when grain prices climbed to record levels, he added.

The agency's latest forecast for 1996 global cereal production was an estimated 1.849 billion tonnes, 6.9 percent higher than the level of 1995. Global wheat output, helped by bumper crops in Europe, was 6.4 percent higher.
FAO said end-of-season cereal carryover stocks were set for their first increase in four years.
"The outlook for global food supplies in 1996/97 has improved somewhat since the last report," it said.
But the picture remained bleak for many, with some countries such as Sierra Leone relying on aid to survive.
The agency said indications also pointed to a further erosion of cereal stocks in the developing countries, which were forecast to fall to their lowest level since 1991.
"In sub-Saharan Africa food supplies for 1996/97 have improved compared to the previous year," FAO said.
"However some 40 percent of the total population of sub-Saharan Africa is already chronically undernourished and this number could rise unless action is taken."
Parts of Liberia were suffering from famine, Somalia had been hit by a combination of drought, insect damage and flooding while Angola and Mozambique had large displaced populations.

"Overall there is a pressing need for large-scale national and international intervention to bring about a rapid improvement in the food security situation of the affected countries," the FAO's special Food Outlook report concluded.
However it warned that global food aid availability in 1996/97 was not expected to improve much from the low 1995/96 level of 7.2 million tonnes.
"Moreover, most low-income food-deficit countries in Africa also face a bleak economic outlook and acute balance of payments difficulties," the FAO report said.
